words.def: Lasting for a very short time.
ex: Fame on social media is often [ephemeral].
The beauty of cherry blossom is [ephemeral], which is part of its charm.
Most of the apps we download are [ephemeral] — used once, then forgotten.
words.nuance: Ephemeral often has a poetic or philosophical tone — beauty, fame, pleasure. Fleeting is used for brief moments (a fleeting glance); transient is more neutral and technical (transient population).
words.ety: Greek ephēmeros 'lasting only a day', from hēmera 'day'.

prec.s: Viral fame is ___: today's internet star is forgotten by next month.
prec.why: Ephemeral suits fame and beauty that vanish quickly. Transient is more technical (transient workers, transient pain); intermittent and sporadic mean happening irregularly.

words.def: Lasting only for a short time; staying in a place only briefly. (n.) A person who stays only briefly.
ex: The side effects are usually mild and [transient].
The city has a large [transient] population of students and seasonal workers.
She reflected on the [transience] of life.
words.nuance: Transient is common in technical contexts (medicine, population, physics) as well as reflective writing. Temporary is the everyday word for things intended to last a short time.
words.ety: Latin transire 'to go across', from trans- 'across' + ire 'to go'.

prec.s: The drug can cause ___ dizziness that usually disappears within an hour.
prec.why: Transient is the standard medical word for a short-lasting symptom. Ephemeral is poetic; provisional means arranged for now but likely to change; makeshift means temporary and improvised (a makeshift shelter).

words.def: Lasting or recurring for a very long time or forever; (of plants) living for several years.
ex: Traffic is a [perennial] problem in this city.
The film is a [perennial] Christmas favourite.
Lavender is a hardy [perennial] that flowers every summer.
words.nuance: Perennial means coming back year after year. Chronic is about a persistent bad condition (chronic pain); enduring is about lasting without fading.
words.ety: Latin perennis 'lasting the year through', from per 'through' + annus 'year'.

prec.s: 'Home Alone' is a ___ favourite, shown on TV every December for over thirty years.
prec.why: A perennial favourite returns year after year. Chronic is for ongoing bad conditions; permanent means unchanging; incessant means non-stop and annoying.

words.def: Something that belongs to a different period of time, especially one that seems old-fashioned now; a chronological error.
ex: In a world of email, the fax machine is an [anachronism].
The film has several [anachronisms], like a wristwatch in ancient Rome.
Some see the monarchy as an expensive [anachronism].
words.nuance: An anachronism is out of its proper time — either outdated or misplaced in a story. A relic is something surviving from the past; a throwback revives older style deliberately.
words.ety: Greek anakhronismos, from ana- 'backwards' + khronos 'time'.

prec.s: The historical drama was mocked online for an obvious ___: a plastic water bottle in a medieval castle.
prec.why: An anachronism is something placed in the wrong time period. A relic and an artefact are genuine objects from the past; an antique is an old valuable object.

words.def: (Of an illness or problem) lasting for a long time or constantly recurring; (of a person) having a habit that is hard to break.
ex: She suffers from [chronic] back pain.
The hospital has a [chronic] shortage of nurses.
He's a [chronic] liar — don't believe a word.
words.nuance: Chronic is the opposite of acute (sudden, severe, short). In British informal speech, 'chronic' can mean 'very bad' — avoid this in formal writing.
words.ety: Greek khronikos 'of time', from khronos.

prec.s: Rural hospitals have suffered a ___ shortage of doctors for over a decade.
prec.why: Chronic describes a long-lasting problem. Acute means sudden and severe; perennial suits recurring favourites or seasonal problems rather than ongoing shortages; temporal means relating to time.

words.def: In an early stage; beginning to happen or develop.
ex: He noticed signs of [incipient] baldness.
The doctor treated the [incipient] infection before it spread.
Investors ignored the [incipient] signs of a crisis.
words.nuance: Incipient is often used for something unwelcome just beginning (a crisis, a disease). Nascent is used for something new and growing, often positive (a nascent industry).
words.ety: Latin incipere 'to begin', from capere 'to take'.

prec.s: The doctor spotted signs of ___ arthritis and recommended exercise to slow it down.
prec.why: Incipient fits the early stage of something unwelcome, like a disease. Nascent, budding and fledgling describe promising things just starting (a budding artist, a fledgling company).

words.def: Just coming into existence and beginning to show signs of future potential.
ex: The country's [nascent] democracy faces many challenges.
Investors are pouring money into the [nascent] space-tourism industry.
She nurtured his [nascent] interest in science.
words.nuance: Nascent is a formal word for something newly born with potential to grow. Fledgling stresses inexperience; embryonic stresses being undeveloped.
words.ety: Latin nasci 'to be born'.

prec.s: The country's ___ electric-car industry received huge government support.
prec.why: Nascent describes a new, promising enterprise. Incipient is usually used for unwelcome developments; infantile means childish; rudimentary means basic and undeveloped.

words.def: Growing or developing quickly.
ex: The city has a [burgeoning] tech scene.
Their [burgeoning] friendship surprised everyone.
Demand for online courses has [burgeoned].
words.nuance: Burgeoning stresses rapid growth or expansion. Flourishing and thriving stress health and success; booming is informal and economic.
words.ety: Old French bourjon 'a bud'.

prec.s: Lisbon's ___ startup scene has grown from a handful of companies to over a thousand in five years.
prec.why: Burgeoning highlights rapid growth — from a handful to a thousand. Nascent and incipient mean just beginning; vibrant means lively, not growing.

words.def: (Of an organisation, industry or custom) in decline and no longer active or effective; (of a person) near death.
ex: The new owner revived the [moribund] newspaper.
Coal mining towns struggled as the industry became [moribund].
Peace talks have been [moribund] for years.
words.nuance: Moribund means close to death, used mostly for institutions and economies. Stagnant means not moving or developing, but not necessarily dying.
words.ety: Latin moribundus, from mori 'to die'.

prec.s: Once the town's pride, the shipyard is now ___, with only a handful of workers left.
prec.why: Moribund means dying, in terminal decline. Stagnant means not developing; dormant means temporarily inactive but able to revive; obsolete means no longer used because something better exists.

words.def: To be forced to stay in an unpleasant situation for a long time; to fail to make progress.
ex: He [languished] in prison for ten years before his release.
The bill has [languished] in committee since spring.
The team is [languishing] at the bottom of the league.
words.nuance: Languish suggests being stuck and neglected, often unjustly. Stagnate means fail to develop, usually of economies or careers.
words.ety: Old French languir, from Latin languere 'to be faint'.

prec.s: The proposal has ___ in a parliamentary committee for two years without a vote.
prec.why: Languish means remain neglected and stuck. Linger means stay longer than expected (by choice); lapse means expire; wilt means droop (plants).

words.def: To decrease gradually in size, strength or importance.
ex: Public interest in the scandal began to [wane].
The moon waxes and [wanes] every month.
His influence is on the [wane].
words.nuance: Wane suggests a gradual, natural decline — like the moon. Dwindle stresses numbers getting smaller; ebb stresses a slow flow away.
words.ety: Old English wanian 'to lessen'.

prec.s: As the novelty wore off, enthusiasm for the new app began to ___.
prec.why: Interest and enthusiasm wane — they gradually lose strength. Dwindle is best for numbers or supplies; shrink is about physical size; subside is about storms, noise or swelling.

words.def: To become gradually smaller in number or amount until little remains.
ex: Our savings [dwindled] during the months without work.
The village population has [dwindled] to a few hundred.
[Dwindling] fish stocks threaten the local economy.
words.nuance: Dwindle is about quantities shrinking, often worryingly (savings, numbers, supplies). Wane is about strength or intensity fading.
words.ety: Diminutive of dwine 'to waste away', from Old English dwinan.

prec.s: With no new members joining, the club's numbers ___ from fifty to just six.
prec.why: Dwindle is ideal for numbers and supplies getting smaller. Wane is for strength, influence or interest; abate and subside are for storms, pain or anger.

words.def: To increase rapidly in number; to spread.
ex: Fake news sites [proliferated] before the election.
Cancer cells [proliferate] uncontrollably.
The treaty aims to stop the [proliferation] of nuclear weapons.
words.nuance: Proliferate suggests rapid multiplication, often of something unwelcome. 'Non-proliferation' is the fixed term in arms control.
words.ety: From proliferation, French prolifère 'producing offspring', from Latin proles 'offspring'.

prec.s: As phone cameras improved, photo-sharing apps ___ — dozens launched every year.
prec.why: Proliferate means multiply rapidly in number. Prosper means succeed financially; accumulate means pile up gradually; escalate means become more intense or serious.

words.def: To make a problem, bad situation or negative feeling worse.
ex: The drought [exacerbated] the food shortage.
Scratching will only [exacerbate] the rash.
His comments [exacerbated] tensions between the two communities.
words.nuance: Exacerbate always makes something already bad worse. Aggravate means the same in formal use, but informally means 'annoy'. Compound means add to a problem.
words.ety: Latin exacerbare 'to irritate', from acerbus 'harsh, bitter'.

prec.s: Cutting interest rates now could ___ inflation, which is already too high.
prec.why: Exacerbate means make an existing problem worse — inflation is 'already too high'. Instigate means start something (an inquiry, a riot); accentuate means emphasise; provoke means cause a reaction.

words.def: To make something bad or unsatisfactory better.
ex: The new law aims to [ameliorate] conditions for factory workers.
Nothing could [ameliorate] the pain of her loss.
Steps were taken to [ameliorate] the effects of the cuts.
words.nuance: Ameliorate means actually improve a bad state. Mitigate and alleviate mean reduce the harm or pain, not necessarily improve the whole situation.
words.ety: French améliorer, from Latin melior 'better'.

prec.s: The charity works to ___ living conditions in refugee camps by building schools and clinics.
prec.why: Ameliorate means improve conditions. Alleviate is for pain or suffering; mollify is for angry people; allay is for fears and suspicions.

words.def: To make suffering, pain or a problem less severe.
ex: The medicine [alleviates] pain but doesn't cure the illness.
Building more homes could help [alleviate] the housing crisis.
Volunteers worked to [alleviate] suffering after the earthquake.
words.nuance: Alleviate is for pain, suffering and pressure already felt. Mitigate is about reducing the severity of a harm or risk. Relieve is the everyday word.
words.ety: Late Latin alleviare 'to lighten', from levis 'light'.

prec.s: A hot bath and some rest helped ___ the pain in her back.
prec.why: Alleviate is the natural verb for relieving pain. Mitigate collocates with risks and impacts; ameliorate with conditions; abate is mostly intransitive (the pain abated).

words.def: (v.) To cause something bad to happen suddenly or sooner than expected. (adj.) Done too quickly, without enough thought.
ex: The scandal [precipitated] the collapse of the government.
Her death [precipitated] a family crisis.
Let's not take any [precipitate] action.
words.nuance: Precipitate means cause something to happen suddenly, often a crisis. Trigger is the everyday word. As an adjective, precipitate means hasty; precipitous means very steep or sudden.
words.ety: Latin praecipitare 'to throw headlong', from caput 'head'.

prec.s: The CEO's sudden resignation ___ a crisis that brought the company close to bankruptcy.
prec.why: Precipitate means cause something to happen suddenly. Preclude means make impossible; precede means come before; presage means be a warning sign of.

words.def: A person or event that causes an important change; (chemistry) a substance that speeds up a reaction.
ex: The protest was the [catalyst] for political reform.
The pandemic acted as a [catalyst] for remote working.
Enzymes are biological [catalysts].
words.nuance: A catalyst speeds up or sparks change. An impetus is a driving force; a trigger is the immediate cause of something (often negative).
words.ety: Greek katalusis 'dissolving'.

prec.s: The pandemic acted as a ___ for remote work, accelerating a change that was already under way.
prec.why: A catalyst speeds up change — the sentence says 'accelerating'. A pretext is a false reason; a precedent is an earlier example; a prerequisite is a necessary condition.

words.def: An event or period marking a turning point; (geography) a ridge dividing two river systems.
ex: The election was a [watershed] in the nation's history.
2007 — the year of the iPhone — was a [watershed] moment for technology.
Her illness marked a [watershed] in her life.
words.nuance: A watershed divides history into before and after. A milestone marks progress along the way; a crossroads is a point where a decision must be made.
words.ety: water + shed 'ridge of high ground', like German Wasserscheide.

prec.s: Historians see 1989 as a ___: after it, Europe would never be the same.
prec.why: A watershed separates history into a clear before and after. A milestone marks progress; a crossroads is a moment of choice; a landmark is an important event or object, but without the 'divide'.

words.def: Unwelcome changes of circumstance or fortune; ups and downs.
ex: Their marriage survived the [vicissitudes] of war and exile.
Small farmers are exposed to the [vicissitudes] of the market.
Her diary records the [vicissitudes] of a long life.
words.nuance: Vicissitudes is almost always plural and literary, especially in 'the vicissitudes of life'. Fluctuations is neutral and technical.
words.ety: Latin vicissitudo, from vicis 'change, turn'.

prec.s: The memoir describes the ___ of a life that took her from poverty to fame and back again.
prec.why: Vicissitudes are the ups and downs of fortune in a life. Fluctuations and oscillations are technical (prices, physics); variations are differences.

words.def: A violent or sudden change or disruption.
ex: Moving to a new country is a major [upheaval] for children.
The 1960s were a period of social [upheaval].
The merger caused enormous [upheaval] in the company.
words.nuance: Upheaval is change that turns things upside down — in society, a company or a life. Turmoil stresses confusion and disorder; cataclysm stresses disaster.
words.ety: up + heave 'to lift'.

prec.s: Divorce and moving house in the same year caused great emotional ___ for the children.
prec.why: 'Emotional upheaval' is a natural collocation for disruption in a life. Revolution is political; cataclysm is a huge disaster; mutation is genetic change.

words.def: (Of an attitude, habit or belief) so firmly established that it is difficult to change.
ex: Racism is deeply [entrenched] in some institutions.
It's hard to change [entrenched] habits.
Both sides have [entrenched] themselves in their positions.
words.nuance: Entrenched suggests something defended against change, like soldiers in trenches. Ingrained suggests habits absorbed deep inside a person.
words.ety: en- + trench, from Old French trenche 'ditch'.

prec.s: Reformers struggled against the ___ interests of powerful families who controlled the industry.
prec.why: 'Entrenched interests' are firmly established and defended. Innate means inborn; inherent means built into the nature of something; inveterate describes a person with a long habit (an inveterate liar).

words.def: Unchanging over time; unable to be changed.
ex: The laws of physics are [immutable].
Traditions are not [immutable]; they evolve over time.
He treats his opinions as [immutable] facts.
words.nuance: Immutable means fundamentally unable to change — laws, truths, principles. Permanent means lasting indefinitely, but could in principle be changed.
words.ety: Latin immutabilis, from mutare 'to change'.

prec.s: Many believe human nature is ___, but history suggests our values shift dramatically.
prec.why: Immutable means unchangeable. Immortal means never dying; imminent means about to happen; impervious means not affected by something.

words.def: Liable to change rapidly and unpredictably, especially for the worse; (of a person) quick to become angry.
ex: Oil prices have been extremely [volatile] this year.
The situation on the border remains [volatile].
He has a [volatile] temper.
words.nuance: Volatile suggests sudden, explosive change — prices, situations, tempers. Erratic suggests irregular, unpredictable behaviour; capricious suggests whim.
words.ety: Latin volatilis 'flying', from volare 'to fly'.

prec.s: Cryptocurrency prices are notoriously ___, sometimes rising or falling 20% in a day.
prec.why: Volatile is the standard financial word for rapid price swings. Capricious and fickle describe people's whims and loyalties; ephemeral means short-lived.

words.def: Based on random choice or personal whim rather than reason or a system.
ex: The deadline seems completely [arbitrary].
Citizens were protected from [arbitrary] arrest.
The order of the list is [arbitrary].
words.nuance: Arbitrary means without principled reasons — it can be neutral (an arbitrary starting point) or critical of unfair power (arbitrary arrest). Random means by chance.
words.ety: Latin arbitrarius, from arbiter 'judge' — originally 'at the judge's discretion'.

prec.s: Human rights law protects citizens against ___ detention by the state.
prec.why: 'Arbitrary detention/arrest' is the legal phrase: detention without lawful reason. Random means by chance; haphazard means disorganised; erratic means irregular.

words.def: Corresponding in size, amount or degree; in proportion.
ex: Salary will be [commensurate] with experience.
The punishment should be [commensurate] with the crime.
She wants a role [commensurate] with her abilities.
words.nuance: Commensurate (with) is formal, typical in job ads and legal writing. Proportionate (to) is the common equivalent.
words.ety: Late Latin commensuratus, from mensurare 'to measure'.

prec.s: Salary: ___ with experience. Please send your CV by Friday.
prec.why: 'Commensurate with experience' is the standard phrase in job ads: in proportion to. Comparable means similar; concurrent means happening at the same time; consistent means unchanging or in agreement.

words.def: Essentially different in kind; not able to be compared.
ex: The festival brings together [disparate] groups of people.
The museum managed to connect such [disparate] subjects as music and maths.
There is a huge [disparity] between rich and poor.
words.nuance: Disparate stresses deep difference, often with the idea of things being brought together. Diverse is positive and inclusive. Disparity (gap, inequality) is very common.
words.ety: Latin disparare 'to separate', from dis- + parare 'to prepare'.

prec.s: The novel weaves together ___ stories — a Victorian sailor, a Korean clone, a 1970s journalist — into one design.
prec.why: Disparate means fundamentally different in kind. Desperate means hopeless; disparaging means belittling; discrete means separate and distinct (individual units), without the stress on difference.

words.def: So small or unimportant that it is not worth considering.
ex: The risk to the public is [negligible].
The cost of the upgrade is [negligible] compared with the benefits.
The difference between the two products is [negligible].
words.nuance: Negligible means small enough to ignore. Don't confuse with negligent (careless in one's duty).
words.ety: Latin neglegere 'to disregard'.

prec.s: The extra weight of the camera is ___; you won't notice it in your bag.
prec.why: Negligible means so small it can be ignored. Negligent means careless; neglected means not cared for; marginal means small but still present or relevant (a marginal improvement).

words.def: More important than anything else; supreme.
ex: Safety is [paramount] in everything we do.
The needs of the child are [paramount].
Trust is of [paramount] importance in a marriage.
words.nuance: Paramount means the most important above all others. Tantamount (to) means 'equivalent to' — a different word often confused with it.
words.ety: Anglo-Norman paramont 'above', from par 'by' + amont 'above'.

prec.s: When designing a children's car seat, safety is ___; everything else comes second.
prec.why: Paramount means more important than anything else. Tantamount means equivalent to; prominent means noticeable; predominant means most common or strongest in number.

words.def: Spreading widely through an area, group or thing, and affecting every part of it.
ex: There was a [pervasive] sense of fear in the city.
The influence of social media is [pervasive].
The smell of smoke [pervaded] the house.
words.nuance: Pervasive means spreading through and affecting every part — often an atmosphere, influence or problem. Ubiquitous is about visible things being everywhere.
words.ety: Latin pervadere 'to go through'.

prec.s: Employees described a ___ culture of fear in which nobody dared to question the boss.
prec.why: Pervasive suits an atmosphere or culture that spreads through everything. Ubiquitous is for visible objects found everywhere; invasive means intruding (invasive species, invasive surgery); prolific means producing a lot.

words.def: (Of something bad) widespread; (rife with) full of something bad.
ex: Corruption is [rife] in the construction industry.
The report is [rife] with errors.
Rumours were [rife] that the director would resign.
words.nuance: Rife is used after a verb ('is rife'), not before a noun. It describes negative things. Rampant adds the sense of spreading out of control.
words.ety: Old English rīfe 'abundant', probably from Old Norse rífr 'acceptable'.

prec.s: The essay is ___ with spelling mistakes; please proofread it before resubmitting.
prec.why: 'Rife with' is used for unwelcome things like errors or corruption. Teeming suits living things; abundant is positive and doesn't take 'with' here; replete means well-filled, often positively.

words.def: A countless or extremely great number; countless.
ex: The city offers [myriad] opportunities for young people.
There are a [myriad] of reasons to learn a language.
[Myriad] stars filled the desert sky.
words.nuance: Myriad can be an adjective ('myriad reasons') or a noun ('a myriad of reasons'); both are accepted today, though some purists prefer the adjective. It sounds more elegant than 'lots of'.
words.ety: Greek murias 'ten thousand'.

prec.s: The app can be customised in ___ ways to suit almost any workflow.
prec.why: Myriad works as an adjective before a plural noun ('myriad ways'). Plethora, multitude and abundance are nouns that need 'a … of'.

words.def: A large or excessive amount of something.
ex: There's a [plethora] of streaming services to choose from.
The report contains a [plethora] of statistics but little analysis.
A [plethora] of rules makes the system hard to navigate.
words.nuance: Plethora originally meant 'too much' and often still suggests an overwhelming amount. Abundance is positive; glut and surfeit are clearly excessive.
words.ety: Greek plēthōrē 'fullness', from plēthein 'to be full'.

prec.s: Faced with a ___ of almost identical shampoo brands, I just picked the cheapest.
prec.why: A plethora is an overwhelming amount. Dearth is a shortage (the opposite); a modicum is a small amount; myriad also means many, but the image of being overwhelmed by too much choice is plethora's.

words.def: A scarcity or lack of something.
ex: There is a [dearth] of affordable housing in the capital.
The [dearth] of evidence made the case hard to prosecute.
There's no [dearth] of opinions on the subject.
words.nuance: Dearth is common in formal writing ('a dearth of talent'). Paucity is more formal still. 'There's no dearth of…' is an ironic way to say 'there's plenty of'.
words.ety: Middle English derthe, from dear 'expensive' — scarcity made things dear.

prec.s: The town's young people leave because of a ___ of jobs and entertainment.
prec.why: A dearth is a lack of something desirable. Plethora means too much; a deficit is a shortfall in money or a measurable amount; deprivation is a state of hardship.

words.def: The presence of something in only small or insufficient quantities.
ex: The [paucity] of data makes firm conclusions impossible.
Critics noted the [paucity] of women in senior roles.
Given the [paucity] of evidence, the case was dropped.
words.nuance: Paucity is academic and formal, often used about evidence, data or information. Dearth is slightly more common and general.
words.ety: Latin paucitas, from paucus 'few'.

prec.s: The authors acknowledge a ___ of long-term data, since the drug is only three years old.
prec.why: Paucity means scarcity, fitting a drug with little long-term data. Plethora means excess; parity means equality; potency means strength.

words.def: Abundant in supply or quantity.
ex: She took [copious] notes during the lecture.
The meal was washed down with [copious] amounts of wine.
He was sweating [copiously] in the heat.
words.nuance: Copious describes a large amount being produced or given, often of liquids or notes. Ample means enough or more than enough; profuse is used for apologies, bleeding and thanks.
words.ety: Latin copiosus, from copia 'plenty' (as in 'cornucopia').

prec.s: During the lecture she took ___ notes, filling twenty pages.
prec.why: 'Copious notes' is a fixed collocation. Profuse is used for apologies, sweating or bleeding; ample means sufficient; lavish suggests expensive generosity.

words.def: (Of a price or amount) unreasonably high.
ex: Hotels charge [exorbitant] prices during the festival.
The bank's fees are [exorbitant].
Rents in the city centre are [exorbitantly] high.
words.nuance: Exorbitant is the standard formal word for unreasonably high prices. Extortionate is stronger, implying exploitation; steep is informal.
words.ety: Latin exorbitare 'to go off the track', from orbita 'wheel track'.

prec.s: Airport cafés charge ___ prices because travellers have no alternative.
prec.why: Exorbitant describes unreasonably high prices. Exuberant means full of energy; extravagant describes spending (or spenders) beyond reason, not the price itself; exhaustive means complete.

words.def: Lacking in quantity or quality; too small. (UK spelling: meagre)
ex: They survived on a [meager] pension.
The results of the campaign were [meager].
Workers were paid a [meager] wage for long hours.
words.nuance: Meager means disappointingly small. Paltry adds contempt (a paltry sum); measly is informal; scanty is used for clothing, evidence and information.
words.ety: Old French maigre 'thin', from Latin macer.

prec.s: After forty years of work, she now lives on a ___ pension of a few hundred dollars a month.
prec.why: A meager pension is too small. Frugal describes careful people or simple meals; scanty suits clothing or evidence; sparse means thinly scattered (sparse vegetation).

words.def: Unnecessary, especially through being more than enough.
ex: Cut any [superfluous] words from your essay.
With GPS, paper maps became almost [superfluous].
I felt [superfluous] at the meeting — nobody needed my input.
words.nuance: Superfluous means beyond what is needed. Redundant also means 'no longer needed' and, in British English, 'dismissed from a job'.
words.ety: Latin superfluus 'overflowing', from super 'over' + fluere 'to flow'.

prec.s: The editor removed every ___ adjective, leaving the prose lean and sharp.
prec.why: Superfluous means beyond what's needed — ideal for unnecessary words. Gratuitous suggests unjustified, often offensive (gratuitous violence); redundant usually refers to repeating something already said; excessive describes amounts, not individual items.

words.def: Done without good reason; unjustified; (formal) free of charge.
ex: Critics complained about the film's [gratuitous] violence.
His comment was a [gratuitous] insult.
The service was [gratuitous], provided by volunteers.
words.nuance: Gratuitous criticises something unnecessary and usually offensive (violence, insults, sex scenes). Superfluous is neutral — just more than needed. A gratuity is a tip.
words.ety: Latin gratuitus 'freely given', from gratia 'favour'.

prec.s: The film was criticised for its ___ violence, which added nothing to the story.
prec.why: 'Gratuitous violence' is violence without justification. Superfluous is a neutral 'more than needed'; gratifying means pleasing; graphic means vividly detailed — which says nothing about justification.

words.def: Outstandingly bad; shocking.
ex: It was an [egregious] error that cost the company millions.
The judge called it an [egregious] abuse of power.
The most [egregious] example of waste was a bridge to nowhere.
words.nuance: Egregious stresses how extremely bad something is. Flagrant stresses that it is done openly, without shame. Glaring stresses that it is obvious.
words.ety: Latin egregius 'standing out from the flock', from grex 'flock' — originally positive.

prec.s: Spending public money on a private yacht was the most ___ example of waste in the report.
prec.why: Egregious means outstandingly bad — a strong condemnation. Conspicuous, prominent and notable describe standing out without saying it's bad.

words.def: (Of a wrong action) conspicuous and shameless.
ex: The arrest was a [flagrant] violation of human rights.
He showed [flagrant] disregard for the rules.
The company [flagrantly] ignored safety regulations.
words.nuance: Flagrant describes rule-breaking done openly. Blatant is very close but more everyday. Fragrant (smelling nice) is a common confusion.
words.ety: Latin flagrare 'to blaze' — hence 'in flagrante delicto', caught in the act.

prec.s: Building the hotel on protected land was a ___ breach of planning law.
prec.why: A flagrant breach is open and shameless. Fragrant means sweet-smelling; flagging means getting tired; fleeting means brief.

words.def: Not harmful or offensive.
ex: It was an [innocuous] question, but she burst into tears.
Most spiders are completely [innocuous].
The message looked [innocuous] but contained a virus.
words.nuance: Innocuous is often used for things that seem harmless but turn out not to be ('a seemingly innocuous remark'). Benign suggests gentleness and kindness.
words.ety: Latin innocuus, from in- 'not' + nocuus 'harmful'.

prec.s: It seemed like an ___ question about holiday plans, but it revealed that he'd been fired.
prec.why: Innocuous means harmless and inoffensive — the expected reading of the question. Innocent describes people; ingenuous means naive; inane means silly.

words.def: Gentle and kind; not harmful; (of a tumour) not cancerous.
ex: Luckily, the tumour turned out to be [benign].
The climate here is [benign] all year round.
He's a [benign] presence in the office.
words.nuance: Benign means harmless or gently kind; in medicine it means not cancerous (opposite: malignant). Benevolent is about actively wishing good.
words.ety: Latin benignus 'kind', from bene 'well'.

prec.s: The doctors were relieved to find the tumour was ___.
prec.why: Benign is the medical term for a non-cancerous growth. Benevolent describes kind people; innocuous describes harmless remarks or substances; beneficial means having good effects.

words.def: Showing signs of future success; favourable.
ex: Winning the first game was an [auspicious] start to the season.
They chose an [auspicious] date for the wedding.
The project got off to an [inauspicious] start when the server crashed.
words.nuance: Auspicious suggests good omens; 'an inauspicious start' is a very common ironic phrase. 'Under the auspices of' means with the support of an organisation.
words.ety: Latin auspex 'bird watcher' — Roman priests predicted the future from birds' flight.

prec.s: The couple chose an ___ date for the wedding, one that astrologers promised would bring good fortune.
prec.why: Auspicious means promising success or good fortune — what the astrologers are looking for. Ominous signals that something bad is coming; portentous means solemnly significant (or pompous); opportune means convenient or well-timed, with no idea of luck or omens.

words.def: Giving the impression that something bad is going to happen.
ex: There was an [ominous] silence after the announcement.
[Ominous] black clouds gathered over the hills.
The engine made an [ominous] noise.
words.nuance: Ominous suggests a warning of trouble to come. Sinister suggests evil intention; menacing suggests a direct threat.
words.ety: Latin omen 'sign, portent'.

prec.s: Just before the crash, the old engine made an ___ grinding noise.
prec.why: Ominous means signalling that something bad is coming. Auspicious signals good things; sinister and malevolent suggest evil intent, which an engine can't have.

words.def: The occurrence of happy or useful events by chance.
ex: Penicillin was discovered by [serendipity].
By pure [serendipity], we sat next to each other on the plane.
Their meeting was entirely [serendipitous].
words.nuance: Serendipity is finding something good while not looking for it. Luck or chance are general; coincidence is two things happening together by chance, not necessarily good.
words.ety: Coined by Horace Walpole (1754) from 'The Three Princes of Serendip', heroes who kept making lucky discoveries.

prec.s: The scientist was looking for a heart drug and discovered Viagra by ___.
prec.why: Serendipity is the happy discovery of something you weren't looking for. Coincidence is two events happening together by chance; destiny and providence suggest fate or God's plan.

words.def: Representing the most perfect or typical example of something.
ex: Fish and chips by the sea is the [quintessential] British experience.
She was the [quintessential] New Yorker: fast, funny and impatient.
The song is [quintessentially] 1980s.
words.nuance: Quintessential means the most perfect example of a type. Archetypal is about the original model of a type; stereotypical is negative and oversimplified.
words.ety: Medieval Latin quinta essentia 'fifth essence' — the pure substance of the heavens.

prec.s: Tea at four o'clock with scones and jam is the ___ English afternoon.
prec.why: Quintessential presents something as the perfect, admirable example. Stereotypical is a negative oversimplification; conventional means following customs; ordinary means unremarkable.

words.def: (Of a work, event or idea) strongly influencing later developments.
ex: Darwin's 'On the Origin of Species' is a [seminal] work.
The band's first album was [seminal] for punk music.
She wrote a [seminal] paper on climate modelling.
words.nuance: Seminal means it planted the seeds of later work — typically books, papers, albums. Groundbreaking stresses novelty; formative stresses shaping during development.
words.ety: Latin seminalis, from semen 'seed'.

prec.s: Her 1985 paper was ___: almost every study in the field since then has built on it.
prec.why: Seminal means hugely influential on later work. Formative describes experiences that shape a person; notorious means famous for something bad; prolific means producing a lot.

words.def: (adj.) Showing great skill; complete or perfect. (v., /ˈkɑːnsəmeɪt/) To complete; to make a marriage complete by having sex.
ex: She's a [consummate] professional who never misses a deadline.
He played the piece with [consummate] skill.
The deal was finally [consummated] in March.
words.nuance: As an adjective, consummate praises complete mastery ('a consummate professional'). It can also be ironic: 'a consummate liar'. Note the different stress for the verb.
words.ety: Latin consummare 'to bring to completion', from summa 'total'.

prec.s: A ___ professional, the actress delivered a flawless performance despite a broken toe.
prec.why: A consummate professional is completely skilled. Consumed means used up or obsessed; consuming means taking up all your time; conspicuous means easily seen.

words.def: Lasting for a long time or longer than expected or usual.
ex: After [protracted] negotiations, the two sides reached a deal.
The war turned into a [protracted] conflict.
She faced a [protracted] legal battle to win custody.
words.nuance: Protracted suggests something dragged out longer than wanted, often painful (negotiations, disputes). Prolonged is more neutral.
words.ety: Latin protrahere 'to prolong', from trahere 'to drag'.

prec.s: After ___ negotiations lasting eighteen months, the union finally accepted the offer.
prec.why: 'Protracted negotiations' is the typical collocation: dragged out over a long time. Chronic is for illnesses and problems; perpetual means never-ending; lingering means slow to disappear.

words.def: (Of something unpleasant or intense) to become less strong or widespread.
ex: We waited for the storm to [abate] before setting off.
The fighting continued [unabated] through the night.
Public anger shows no sign of [abating].
words.nuance: Abate is used for storms, pain, anger, crises — intense things losing force. Subside is very similar; dwindle is about numbers.
words.ety: Old French abatre 'to beat down'.

prec.s: We sheltered in a café, waiting for the storm to ___ before walking home.
prec.why: Storms, anger and pain abate: they lose their force. Dwindle is for numbers and supplies; wane is for influence, interest or the moon; diminish is neutral and usually needs a measurable quantity.
